title: Histoplasmosis
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Histoplasmosis is a dimorphic fungal infection acquired by inhaling microconidia from bird or bat‑contaminated soil. It ranges from asymptomatic to severe disseminated disease, especially in immunocompromised patients.

sections.p: Histoplasma capsulatum is a thermally dimorphic fungus; mould in the environment and yeast in human tissue. Infection is usually acquired by inhalation of airborne microconidia from soil enriched with bird or bat droppings.
b: 90% of exposures are asymptomatic or mild flu‑like illness
Endemic in Ohio/Mississippi River valleys, parts of Africa, Latin America and other tropical regions

sections.p: In the environment the fungus grows as a mould producing tuberculate macroconidia. At 37 °C it converts to a small (2–5 µm) budding yeast that can survive inside macrophages.
b: Grows on Sabouraud agar; characteristic tuberculate macroconidia

sections.p: Microconidia become aerosolised when contaminated soil is disturbed. Inhaled spores reach alveoli, are phagocytosed, and convert to yeast, spreading via the reticulo‑endothelial system.
b: Inhalation of dust from bird roosts, bat caves, chicken coops
Rarely transmitted by organ transplantation or cutaneous inoculation

sections.p: Clinical manifestations depend on inoculum size and host immunity. Acute pulmonary histoplasmosis mimics a mild pneumonia; chronic pulmonary disease resembles tuberculosis; disseminated disease involves multiple organs and is life‑threatening in HIV, transplant or steroid‑treated patients.
b: Acute pulmonary: fever, cough, chest pain, hilar lymphadenopathy
Chronic pulmonary: cough, weight loss, upper‑lobe cavitary lesions, similar to TB
Disseminated: fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, adrenal insufficiency, mucocutaneous lesions

sections.p: Combine clinical suspicion with targeted investigations. In low‑resource settings, microscopy and antigen testing are most useful; culture and histopathology are confirmatory when available.
b: If antigen test unavailable, rely on microscopy of sputum, BAL, or tissue
In HIV patients, a single positive antigen test is sufficient to start therapy

t.b: Shows whether infiltrates are focal, miliary, or cavitary – helps differentiate acute vs chronic disease
Detects circulating antigen; positive in >90% of disseminated disease – useful when culture unavailable

t.a: Peripheral blood smear or bone‑marrow aspirate (Giemsa stain)
t.b: Looks for intracellular yeast; confirms disseminated infection
Gold standard but may take 4‑6 weeks; not practical for urgent decisions
Detects antibodies; rises after 2‑4 weeks – limited in early disease or immunosuppressed

sections.p: Treat severe pulmonary, chronic pulmonary, or disseminated disease with itraconazole; liposomal amphotericin B is reserved for life‑threatening cases. Supportive care includes fluid management and monitoring for adrenal crisis.
b: Itraconazole – oral, fungistatic, good tissue penetration; first‑line for most forms
Liposomal amphotericin B – rapid fungicidal action; used in severe or CNS disease
Monitor liver function and drug interactions (e.g., with antiretrovirals)

sections.p: Key points examiners love: epidemiology, dimorphic nature, diagnostic algorithm in resource‑limited settings, drug choice rationale, and distinguishing features from TB and other endemic mycoses.
b: Most infections are self‑limited; treatment is indicated for moderate‑severe, chronic, or disseminated disease
Disseminated histoplasmosis is an AIDS‑defining illness; look for adrenal insufficiency
Urine antigen is the quickest test for disseminated disease

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive respiratory distress or shock
Signs of adrenal crisis (hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia)

faq.q: Why is histoplasmosis common in HIV patients?
faq.a: Cell‑mediated immunity is impaired, allowing uncontrolled replication of intracellular yeast and dissemination.

faq.q: Can a negative chest X‑ray rule out histoplasmosis?
faq.a: No; early disease may have a normal radiograph, especially in immunocompetent hosts.

faq.q: What is the most specific laboratory finding?
faq.a: Intracellular budding yeast seen on tissue biopsy or bone‑marrow aspirate.

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer with HIV presents with fever, weight loss, and hepatosplenomegaly – what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Order urine Histoplasma antigen; it is rapid and highly sensitive for disseminated disease.
How does the dimorphic switch of Histoplasma aid its pathogenicity? — Yeast form survives inside macrophages, evading host defenses.

A patient with chronic cough and upper‑lobe cavitary lesions lives near a bat cave; how do you differentiate TB from chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis? — Compare sputum AFB smear, culture, and Histoplasma antigen; TB shows acid‑fast bacilli, histoplasmosis shows negative AFB and positive antigen.
Why is itraconazole preferred over fluconazole for histoplasmosis? — Itraconazole has superior activity against Histoplasma; fluconazole’s MICs are high.
In a resource‑limited hospital without antigen testing, what is the best way to confirm disseminated histoplasmosis? — Perform Giemsa‑stained bone‑marrow aspirate looking for intracellular yeast.
What complications should you monitor for during treatment of disseminated histoplasmosis? — Adrenal insufficiency, hepatic toxicity from itraconazole, and drug interactions with ART.

A patient on long‑term steroids develops fever and diffuse skin papules; what feature points toward histoplasmosis rather than cutaneous leishmaniasis? — Presence of intracellular yeast on skin biopsy and positive urine antigen.
When is amphotericin B indicated in histoplasmosis and what are its main risks? — Severe disseminated or CNS disease; risks include nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbances.
